findings.element: states.print in render-b.js, foot({ link: F.shareUrl }), rendered through .b-foot span in b.css
findings.problem: The A4 sheet is described as the keepsake, the thing that gets pinned up in the venue kitchen and kept in a box afterwards, and the last line printed on it is timeline.signalstudio.ie/s/j7Qm2vK4xR9bT1nL6yH3cW8pZ5sD0aG7fJ4uE2rN9tM set in 11px mono with text-transform: uppercase. Driving state=print, the source string is mixed case and the rendered string is TIMELINE.SIGNALSTUDIO.IE/S/J7QM2VK4XR9BT1NL6YH3CW8PZ5SD0AG7FJ4UE2RN9TM. The token is case sensitive, so the only version of the link that exists on paper is the one version that cannot work: anyone who types what is printed lands on the ended screen, which then tells them in good faith that the couple turned the link off. Even if the case survived, forty-three random characters is not a thing a person transcribes, and printing a share secret on a sheet that gets handed around a venue is a decision nobody made on purpose. This is the one surface with no undo, no live region and no way to correct itself, and it is carrying the product's only broken fact.
findings.fix: In states.print change foot({ link: F.shareUrl }) to foot({ link: "timeline.signalstudio.ie" }), so the sheet names the place and not the secret. If the sheet must carry a way back in, it goes above the footer as a real sentence rather than a micro-label: h("p.b-printLink", { text: "The live plan is at " + F.shareUrl }) with .b-print .b-printLink { text-transform: none; letter-spacing: 0; font-size: 12px; word-break: break-all; } so at least the characters printed are the characters that work. Add two gate assertions on state=print: document.body.innerText does not contain F.token in upper case, and getComputedStyle on whatever node carries F.token reports textTransform none.

findings.element: states.day in render-b.js: the .b-dayNote paragraph, the .b-dayNow label, and the dayOf branch of behindBlock()
findings.problem: This is the screen the whole company is judged on and it is still written as a status page. Under the couple's names and the word Today it says "This is the day the plan was for.", which is past tense about the plan on the morning of the thing itself. Then a section headed HAPPENING NOW over "Wedding day at The Orchard", which is a database state label (MILESTONE_STATE_LABELS.now, verbatim) used as prose, and which is simply untrue at eight in the morning when most people will open this. Then the block that closes the page: HOW YOU GOT HERE, 8 MOMENTS, and one sentence, "Venue walk-through, 19 September." The dayOf branch takes done[done.length - 1], the most recent thing, so the last words a couple and their families read before the footer on their wedding morning are the name of an admin task from a fortnight earlier. The label was rewritten last round and the sentence under it was not, so the heading now promises an arc and delivers the tail of a to-do list.
findings.fix: Three edits in render-b.js. (1) Delete the h("p.b-dayNote", ...) line: Today, the names, Saturday 3 October 2026 and the section beneath already say everything, and the sentence only weakens them. (2) In the dayOf branch of behindBlock change note = last.title... to note = done[0].title + ", " + F.fmt.medium(done[0].date) + "." so "How you got here" opens where it actually started, "We said yes, 2 January.", using the same title-comma-date grammar the guest note already uses. (3) Change the .b-dayNow label from "Happening now" to "Where to be", which is true at any hour and is the one fact a guest opening this on the morning is looking for; update the gate assertion at interaction-check.mjs line 699 from /happening now/i to /where to be/i, leaving the /wedding day/i half untouched. Add an assertion that state=day text ends on done[0].title and contains no MILESTONE_STATE_LABELS value.

findings.element: gapSentence() and horizon() in render-b.js: .b-gapNote, and the pair .b-todayLabel plus .b-origin
findings.problem: On the received phone the fourth thing the reader meets, directly under the indigo rule, is "Nothing is planned until 1 August." Forty pixels below it, seven planned things are listed by name and date. The sentence is not a soft framing, it is false on its own page, and it is the sentence a couple's mother reads first. It also carries the owner's grammar onto the audience's screen: a planner thinks in empty weeks, the people receiving this think in what is coming. The same block says today twice in two grammars, TODAY IS 16 JULY under the rule and TODAY, 16 JULY at the head of the rail, one hundred and forty pixels apart on a 390px screen, which is the one-grammar-per-fact class from the defect library reappearing inside a single header. Both strings ride every guest surface: phone, desk and the printed sheet.
findings.fix: In gapSentence return "The next thing is " + F.fmt.medium(nearestIso) + "." It stays a boundary rather than a count, so it still cannot go off by one and the existing assertion that the note is not "The next 16 days" still holds. Then delete the h("p.b-todayLabel", ...) line from horizon() and remove "aria-hidden": "true" from the .b-origin push in measure(), so today is stated exactly once, at the top of the rail where it anchors the instrument, and it is in the accessibility tree. states.loading builds its own .b-todayLabel directly and is unaffected. Add a gate assertion that (document.body.innerText.match(/today/gi) || []).length === 1 on states phone, desk and print.

findings.element: setTitle() and the name === "add" branch of wireOwner() in render-b.js
findings.problem: setTitle displays value.trim() || "Untitled moment" but writes record.title = value.trim(), so the row and the record hold different strings the moment a title is empty, and every sentence built from the record loses its subject. Driving it: clear the title field, and the row reads "Untitled moment" while the reversibility bar reads " moved 7 days later." with a leading space and no subject, the delete receipt reads " was removed.", the editor announces itself as "Editing " and the row's own button is named "Open . Thursday 17 September, in 63 days. Shown to guests." The newly built add path arrives in exactly this state: press Add a moment and the editor's accessible name is "Editing " and the new row's button is "Open . Saturday 25 July, in 9 days." So the feature this round was built to deliver introduces itself, to a screen reader, as nothing. The gate cannot see it because it only drives the happy path where a title is typed.
findings.fix: In setTitle change record.title = value.trim() to record.title = shown, so one string serves the row, the receipt, the panel name and the button name. In the add branch set fresh.title = "Untitled moment" rather than "", keep the input.value = "" line so the field still opens empty and typing replaces the placeholder name, and change the history sentence from "A moment was added." to "An untitled moment was added." so the receipt names what it made. Add gate assertions: after clearing #b-edit-title, .b-undoText and .b-edit[aria-label] both begin with "Untitled moment"; after pressing Add a moment, no element's accessible name is empty or begins with a space.

findings.element: the setday handler in states["owner-empty"] of render-b.js and #b-empty-hint
findings.problem: The editor refuses in three precise sentences: "That is not a date. Try 3 October 2026.", "That day has gone. Pick one still ahead.", "This is as far as it goes. Wedding day is the last day." The empty project, which is the first screen anyone ever sees in this product, refuses in one, "Type the day first. For example, 3 October 2026.", and it fires that sentence at someone who did type: typing banana returns it verbatim, telling a person who has just typed to type. Worse, the field accepts a wedding day that has already gone. Typing 1 January 2020 returns "The day is set. Moments come next.", so the product's very first act is to cheerfully accept a wedding six years in the past, on the one field it has just said everything else is measured from. The product speaks well on screen four and badly on screen one, which is exactly the wrong way round.
findings.fix: Replace the handler body with a branch that reuses the editor's exact words, so there is one refusal vocabulary in the product: if (!input.value.trim()) refuse("Type the day first. For example, 3 October 2026."); else if (!F.parseDay(input.value)) refuse("That is not a date. Try 3 October 2026."); else if (F.days(F.today, F.parseDay(input.value)) < 1) refuse("That day has gone. Pick one still ahead."); else accept("The day is set. Moments come next.") — where refuse sets aria-invalid true, writes #b-empty-hint and returns focus to the field, exactly as now. Add gate assertions on owner-empty: "banana" yields aria-invalid true and the words "That is not a date"; "1 January 2020" yields aria-invalid true and the words "That day has gone"; "3 October 2026" yields aria-invalid false.

biggestWin: The reversibility bar now speaks English, and that is the thing this round actually bought. Every gesture in the owner surface comes back as a sentence a person would say out loud, in the same words as the button that caused it: "Send the invitations moved 7 days earlier.", "Renamed to Send the invitations to everyone.", "Send the invitations is now hidden from guests.", "Send the invitations was removed." One fact, one grammar, one direction word shared between the control and its receipt, and the refusals hold the same line: "That day has gone. Pick one still ahead." is eight words that state the rule, the reason and the next move without a single apology or piece of jargon. Around it the voice at rest is still the best material in the lab. "Kept by Orla" turns a timestamp into a person taking responsibility. "It carries the day, the distance and the plan, and nothing from your workspace: no notes, no suppliers, no prices" answers the only question a planner has about sharing, before they ask it. "Here is everything, love. It updates itself." is six words carrying the whole promise, written the way a planner actually texts. "Bringing in what is ahead." refuses the shimmer register outright. And the split in behindBlock, where the owner gets a tally and the guest gets the thing itself, is judgement rather than word choice: a couple who have never used a tracker are never handed a score. The palette is spent, not merely obeyed. Across a whole received phone screen indigo appears exactly twice, as the rule under the horizon and the one filled tick on the next thing, and it never sets a letter, so the accent still means something on the eleventh screen. That is the test almost every ink-and-white product fails by the third.
